say.text: Last stretch. You build the summary, I only check it. Start with the backbone.
Which set lists the four components of classic TOF?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy
VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, atrial septal defect
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, left ventricular hypertrophy

say.text: Think of the anterior septum, the aorta's position, the outflow narrowing and the chamber that has to push against it. No extra holes, no left side.
Yes. A large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
The ASD is tempting because it is a common extra hole, and old PYQs keyed ASD, PDA and LVH as 'not part of TOF'.
But the four components include no ASD, PDA or LVH. ASD and PDA may accompany TOF. The fourth component is right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: ASD and PDA accompany TOF at times, but they are not among the four.

say.text: LVH is tempting because 'ventricular hypertrophy' sounds the same on either side.
But the thick ventricle in TOF is the right one: right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the side: TOF loads the right ventricle, so the fourth component is right ventricular hypertrophy.

say.text: RVH is the last of the four, and it is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Why does it come last in the chain?

choices.label: It is a consequence: the RV works against high pressure
It is a primary defect, malformed along with the septum
The LV carries extra volume and hypertrophies, pushing the RV

say.text: Ask which comes first in time: a high-pressure load on the right ventricle, or the thick wall.
Right. The RV hypertrophies as a consequence of chronic systemic pressures, so it follows from the VSD and the obstruction rather than starting the chain.
This is tempting because the other three components look like birth defects of the same malalignment.
But RVH is described as secondary to chronic systemic pressures, so it is an effect, not a cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause: the septal and outflow lesions are the structural defects. RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

say.text: A volume-loaded left heart is the usual story in other shunts, so it is tempting.
But in TOF the hypertrophy is on the right, and it is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the side: TOF thickens the right ventricle, not the left.

say.text: An echo of a cyanotic 6-month-old shows an anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, sub-pulmonary narrowing, a thick RV wall and a small ASD.
Which finding is an accompanying lesion rather than one of the four?
Three of these match the four-part list you just picked. One is a hole in a different septum.
Yes. ASD and PDA are among the anomalies that may accompany TOF. The four components include no ASD, PDA or LVH.
It is tempting because the aorta sits over a defect, which feels like an add-on.
But an overriding aorta is one of the four classic components.
The ASD is the one that only may accompany TOF.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so see the list again: the overriding aorta is component two. The ASD is the extra.

say.text: It is tempting because the thick wall develops later, so it can feel like an add-on.
But right ventricular hypertrophy is the fourth component, even though it is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
The ASD is the accompanying lesion.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: secondary does not mean optional. RVH is still one of the four.

say.text: The TOF ECG shows right axis deviation and prominent R or qR waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Which explanation fits that tracing?

choices.label: The RV is hypertrophied, so right-sided forces dominate
The LV is hypertrophied from extra pulmonary flow
Pulmonary plethora is overloading the left atrium

say.text: Which ventricle is thick? The ECG simply reports the thick side.
Right. The tracing is characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy. The film agrees, with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
Left-sided changes are tempting from other shunts, where extra flow loads the left heart.
But in TOF most blood shunts to the aorta, bypassing the lungs, so the film shows pulmonary oligaemia, and the ECG shows right-sided change.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck: TOF sends blood away from the lungs. Pulmonary oligaemia and right axis go together.

say.text: Plethora is tempting because a VSD sounds like extra lung flow.
But with significant RVOT obstruction, blood bypasses the pulmonary bed, and the film shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so see it again: TOF is oligaemic, not plethoric.

say.text: A child with TOF goes into a tet spell. Spells need a rapid and aggressive approach.
Which sequence is right?

choices.label: Knee-chest and oxygen, then IV fluids, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine
Phenylephrine, then morphine, then knee-chest and oxygen
Oxygen, then IV furosemide, then digoxin

say.text: Bedside measures that need no drip come first. Then volume. Then the drugs.
Yes. Knee-chest positioning, oxygen, IV fluid boluses, then IV beta-blockers or IV phenylephrine, with morphine as a sedative.
Starting with a drug feels aggressive enough for a crisis, which is tempting.
But the bedside measures, knee-chest positioning and oxygen, head the list. Drugs come after them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause: the list opens with knee-chest positioning and oxygen, before any IV drug.

say.text: A blue, breathless child looks like heart failure, so a diuretic and digoxin tempt.
But the listed measures are fluid boluses to improve RV filling, beta-blockers and phenylephrine. Furosemide is not among them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reframe it: a spell is about RV filling and systemic resistance, not congestion.

say.text: Knee-chest positioning is given to increase systemic vascular resistance.
Why does that help a child in a spell?

choices.label: Blood is steered toward the lungs when systemic resistance rises
It lowers pulmonary vascular resistance directly
It lowers systemic afterload so the RV empties easily

say.text: Blood chooses between two exits, the RVOT and the aorta. Which exit does squatting make harder?
Right. Blood takes the path of lower resistance. If RVOT resistance is below systemic, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic, so raising systemic resistance pushes the balance that way.
Pulmonary resistance is tempting because oxygen does cause pulmonary vasodilation.
But positioning is the systemic lever: it increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the levers: oxygen acts on the pulmonary side, knee-chest on the systemic side.

say.text: Lowering afterload is a standard move in heart failure, which is why it tempts.
But the aim here is the opposite: to increase systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse it: a spell is treated by raising systemic resistance, not lowering it.

say.text: IV phenylephrine is given in a spell to increase systemic afterload.
It raises afterload, so why is it a good drug here?

choices.label: Higher systemic resistance steers blood away from the aorta
It dilates the pulmonary vessels like oxygen
It strengthens a failing RV, like an inotrope

say.text: Same side of the balance as squatting. Which resistance does it raise?
Yes. The same lever as knee-chest: raise systemic resistance relative to the RVOT, and less blood bypasses the lungs.
Pulmonary vasodilation is tempting as the spell goal, and oxygen provides it.
But phenylephrine works on the systemic side: it increases systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort them: oxygen is the pulmonary vasodilator, phenylephrine the systemic lever.

say.text: Heart-failure thinking makes an inotrope tempting.
But the spell measures target RV filling and systemic resistance, and phenylephrine's stated job is to increase systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so drop the heart-failure frame: the stated aim is to increase systemic afterload.

say.text: The echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis of TOF.
Why does it earn that place?

choices.label: It directly shows the abnormal anatomy
It is the more invasive test, so it is more definitive
It shows everything, so CT and MRI add nothing

say.text: The reason is in the name of the job: it looks directly at the heart.
Right. Echocardiography allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy and remains the primary diagnostic modality.
Catheterisation is tempting as a gold standard because invasive tests feel more definitive.
But echocardiography is the gold standard, through direct visualisation of the anatomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: the gold standard here is the echocardiogram, not an invasive test.

say.text: The first half is true, which makes this tempting.
But contrast-enhanced CT shows the complex cardiovascular morphology, and MRI gives anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep both: echo diagnoses, and CT and MRI each add a job.

say.text: Which pairing of test and job is right in TOF?

choices.label: Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation
MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo for follow-up only
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only

say.text: Yes. Echocardiography is the primary diagnostic modality, and MRI gives anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.
MRI sounds comprehensive, so first-line feels plausible.
But echocardiography remains the primary diagnostic modality. MRI adds anatomy and function without radiation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reorder: echo first, MRI as the added layer.

say.text: Catheterisation is tempting because it is the old image of a definitive test.
But the echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck: echo is the gold standard, not a screen.

say.text: After TOF repair, which is the most common indication for reoperation?
Think of what the surgeon reconstructs at the outflow, and what can leak afterwards.
Yes. Pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation, and valve replacement can be surgical or transcatheter.
A leftover VSD is tempting because the patch is the obvious repair site.
But pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation after repair.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: the late problem is pulmonary insufficiency.

say.text: It is tempting because the obstruction was what you removed.
But the most common indication for reoperation is pulmonary insufficiency.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: the commonest reoperation is for pulmonary insufficiency.

say.text: Pulmonary insufficiency leads reoperations after repair.
Why does pulmonary regurgitation follow repair?

choices.label: It results from reconstruction of the RVOT

say.text: Right. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT.
The patch is the other repair site, which makes this tempting.
But the stated source of pulmonary regurgitation is reconstruction of the RVOT.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so relink: the regurgitation comes from the outflow reconstruction.

say.text: Failure of a pump is a familiar cause of valve problems, which tempts.
But pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: the cause is the RVOT reconstruction.

say.text: Last one, and the sneakiest.
About what share of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias?
Yes. 40 to 50 percent of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias. Sudden death risk is 6 to 9 percent at 30 years, and endocarditis risk remains.
It is tempting because repair feels like a cure.
But 40 to 50 percent of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death risk is 6 to 9 percent 30 years on.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep this: repair is not a cure. Arrhythmia risk stays.

say.text: A good result suggests a clean heart, so this tempts.
But arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, can occur after repair, and patients with repaired or unrepaired TOF are at risk of endocarditis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: a repaired TOF still carries arrhythmia and endocarditis risk.

say.text: One malaligned septum, a narrowed infundibulum, a right ventricle working against it. Echo diagnoses, bedside levers treat the spell, and repair leaves a lifelong follow-up.

cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy.

cards.q: Is ASD one of the four components?
cards.a: No. ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among the four.

cards.q: Why is RVH last in the chain?
cards.a: It is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Right axis deviation with prominent R or qR in V1; decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echocardiography; CT shows complex morphology, MRI anatomy and function without radiation.
Knee-chest (raises SVR), oxygen (pulmonary vasodilation), IV fluids (RV filling), then beta-blocker or phenylephrine.

cards.q: Commonest reoperation after repair, and its source?
cards.a: Pulmonary insufficiency, from reconstruction of the RVOT.

cards.q: Ventricular arrhythmia share in repaired adults?
cards.a: 40-50%; sudden death 6-9% at 30 years; endocarditis risk persists.
